title: Not annihilation (section 27)
hook: don't think the bodhisattva destroys things; emptiness is not nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, form and sound: the verse that says the Tathagata isn't found by the eye's catch or the ear's catch, but seen from the Dharma. Your line: not by form or sound. Whom did you see past the surface? Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

Somewhere tonight a college sophomore reads one chapter of Buddhist philosophy, shuts the book, and announces to the roommate: nothing is real. So the dishes don't matter. The roommate, who has seen the sink, has thoughts. It's an old wrong turn, and the Diamond Sutra has been walking right past it for weeks now. No self, no being, no marks, no merit held, no teaching owned. Keep cutting like that and someone will decide the whole thing is a wrecking ball. In section twenty-seven, the Buddha stops and blocks that road by name. Today: not annihilation.
screen: `NOTHING IS REAL, SO NO DISHES.` → `ALL THAT CUTTING.` → `A ROAD BLOCKED BY NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the danger. The sutra has cut almost everything a person could hold: a self, the bodily marks, merit, the teaching itself, even the raft. A listener could come away thinking the bodhisattva's job is to tear things down. Second, the line. In paraphrase, the Buddha tells Subhuti: don't think the highest awakening was reached through the marks. And then, let no one tell you that those who set out on the bodhisattva path teach the destruction of anything, or its annihilation. Not of a single thing. The cutting was never demolition. Third, the middle road. This isn't a new idea dropped in at the end. In an early discourse, the Buddha tells a monk named Kaccana that the view everything exists is one extreme, and the view nothing exists is the other. The Tathagata, he says, teaches by the middle, without going to either one. Section twenty-seven stands on that same ground. When the sutra says a thing has no fixed self, it hasn't said the thing is gone. Fourth, what that leaves in your hands. Empty, in this teaching, means empty of a fixed, separate core. It doesn't mean empty of being here. A cup that is only so called still holds the tea. The bodhisattva who frees no beings is still at work helping them. So the roommate is right, and so, in a way, is the sutra. Nothing is fixed. The dishes are still real. And somebody still has to wash them.
screen: `ALL THAT CUTTING.` · `NO THING DESTROYED.` · `THE MIDDLE, NOT THE EXTREMES.` · `EMPTY OF A CORE, STILL HERE.` · then, large: `NOT NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor one real thing. Settle, and breathe. Let your attention land on one ordinary thing near you: the chair holding you up, the floor under your feet, a plant on the sill. Notice that it has no fixed core you could pull out and keep. It's made of other things, and it's changing. Then notice, just as clearly, that it's here. It's warm, or worn, or doing its job. Let both be true at once. If you'd like, give it a small sign of respect: rest your palm on it, or simply say thank you inside. The bell holds the time.
Not annihilation. Section twenty-seven: those on the bodhisattva path don't teach the destruction of anything. Empty of a fixed core is not the same as nothing. Today's word.
Your line: not nothing. Today, when something feels like it doesn't matter, give it one moment of real care anyway: a dish, a reply, a hello. Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers present emptiness as a middle way between the views that everything exists and that nothing exists, and section 27 of the Diamond Sutra is read as a guard against hearing emptiness as nothingness.

pairs: the monk told about the middle

myth: the bodhisattva path teaches the destruction of things
section 27 says no one should claim it teaches the annihilation of anything.
the Buddha called 'nothing exists' an extreme
in the discourse to Kaccana, alongside 'everything exists'; he teaches by the middle.
empty means not there at all
empty of a fixed, separate core, not empty of being here.

fork.setup: after all the sutra's cutting, a friend says: so the bodhisattva path destroys everything. what does section 27 say?
options: no: they don't teach the annihilation of anything
only the bad things get destroyed
fork.reveal: the Buddha says let no one tell you that those on the bodhisattva path teach the destruction or annihilation of any thing.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: cutting off, annihilation; the extreme section 27 says the bodhisattva path does not teach.

trapdoor: what you thought: emptiness means nothing is really there.
what it means: things lack a fixed core; they aren't destroyed or erased.
what a scholar hears: section 27 guards against the annihilation view, the extreme the Buddha sets beside 'everything exists' in the Kaccana discourse.

notes: Section 27 paraphrased, not quoted from Max Müller (wording unverified): check both halves (awakening not through the marks; no destruction or annihilation of any dharma taught by those on the bodhisattva path).
Kaccanagotta Sutta (SN 12.15) paraphrased: 'everything exists' and 'nothing exists' as two extremes, the Tathagata teaching by the middle. Confirm.
Original-language word: uccheda as the Sanskrit term for annihilation in section 27 (alongside vinasa); confirm the term in the Sanskrit text and the pronunciation.
'Empty of a fixed, separate core' is a teaching gloss on emptiness, not a quotation; confirm the fair description.

Editor: fixed a garbled line (the sutra never speaks of a cup) and cut the shoveling image, which borrowed day 1142's neighbors as if they were the bodhisattva; changed practice objects (mug, hand) that repeated day 1134.
